title: Rotating black holes
one_line_summary: Builds the Kerr metric from Schwarzschild with the Newman-Janis complex-shift trick on a null tetrad, then reads off its rotation, ring singularity, two horizons, ergosphere, principal null congruences and global structure for sub-extremal, extremal and super-extremal spin, before closing the black-hole part of the book with Kerr-Newman, no-hair, the Penrose process, Komar and ADM mass, the singularity theorems and Hawking radiation.
role_in_book: Final chapter of the black-hole sequence (ch15 Schwarzschild, ch16 classical tests, ch17 horizons and Eddington-Finkelstein charts, ch18 Kruskal and Penrose diagrams, ch19 Reissner-Nordstrom). It deliberately reuses the whole Schwarzschild/RN toolkit - redshift surfaces from g_00, horizons from g^11 = 0, null congruences, Eddington-Finkelstein extension, conformal diagrams - on the first non-spherical solution, so that genuinely rotational features (frame dragging, ergosphere, ring singularity, closed timelike curves) stand out against a familiar background. Its last three sections widen into a survey of global results (mass at infinity, singularity theorems, black-hole thermodynamics) that link back to the 3+1 formalism of ch14 and forward to the null focusing equation (23.44) of ch23 on radiation from isolated sources and black-body radiation (ch26).

learning_objectives: Reader can build a null tetrad (l, n, m, m-bar) from an orthonormal tetrad, verify its null and normalization conditions, and write g_ab and g^ab as sums of tetrad products.

Reader can describe the Newman-Janis procedure (complexify r, rewrite the Schwarzschild tetrad, shift v and r by i a cos(theta), demand reality) and state honestly that it is a generating trick rather than a derivation from the field equations.
Reader can write the Kerr metric in advanced Eddington-Finkelstein, Boyer-Lindquist and Kerr (Kerr-Schild) forms and state which one is convenient for which question.

Reader can give three pieces of evidence that the Kerr parameter a encodes rotation: the t -> -t, phi -> -phi invariance, the dt dphi cross term matching a rotating-frame metric, and the 1/R expansion identifying angular momentum ma.
Reader can explain why the Boyer-Lindquist r is not the Euclidean radius and derive R^2 = r^2 + a^2 sin^2(theta) and asymptotic flatness.
Reader can locate the ring singularity, the infinite-redshift surfaces S_+/- (from g_00 = 0) and the horizons r_+/- (from g^11 = Delta = 0), and sketch how they nest, including the ergosphere.
Reader can find the principal null congruences by exploiting the t and phi first integrals and the null condition, and use them to build Eddington-Finkelstein-type coordinates regular across r = r_+.

Reader can show from the photon-orbit condition dr = dtheta = ds^2 = 0 that no observer can stay at rest relative to infinity inside S_+, and explain why S_+ is called the stationary limit surface and is crossable both ways.

Reader can read the Penrose diagrams of Kerr for a^2 < m^2 and a^2 = m^2 (regions I, II, III, negative r, timelike ring, closed timelike curves) and describe the super-extremal case as a naked singularity motivating cosmic censorship.
Reader can state the Kerr-Newman parameters, its horizon condition a^2 + epsilon^2 <= m^2, and the content (and status) of the no-hair/uniqueness result.
Reader can describe the Penrose process qualitatively and say where the extracted energy comes from.

Reader can compute total charge as a surface integral at infinity and use the same template to define and evaluate the Komar mass of Schwarzschild; reader can quote the ADM mass integral and the positive energy theorem.

Reader can list the three ingredients of a pattern singularity theorem, state the timelike/null convergence and strong/weak energy conditions, and explain why the theorems prove geodesic incompleteness rather than infinite curvature.

Reader can state the black-hole thermodynamic analogies (area-entropy, surface gravity-temperature) and evaluate the Hawking temperature T = hbar c^3 / (8 pi G k_B M), noting that it falls as mass grows.

teaching_approach.summary: A two-speed chapter. Sections 20.1-20.10 are a careful, component-level replay of the Schwarzschild and Reissner-Nordstrom programme on the Kerr metric: the metric is obtained by a stated trick rather than by solving the field equations, then interrogated with exactly the same diagnostics the reader already trusts (g_00 = 0 for infinite redshift, g^11 = 0 for null r = const surfaces, first integrals for null geodesics, a congruence-adapted coordinate change for extension, conformal diagrams by analogy with RN). Physical interpretation is built from suggestive arguments - discrete symmetries, a flat-space rotating-frame cross term, a large-R expansion - explicitly labelled as non-rigorous. Sections 20.11-20.14 switch to a descriptive survey of results the book cannot prove at its level (no-hair, Penrose process, positive energy, singularity theorems, Hawking radiation), with one fully worked calculation (Komar mass of Schwarzschild) motivated by an electromagnetic Gauss-law analogy. Many derivations are pushed into '(exercise)' markers keyed to the 18 end-of-chapter exercises.
narrative_arc: Motivation: solving the vacuum equations directly for a rotating black hole is long, so obtain Kerr (and later Kerr-Newman) by a complex transformation instead; this needs null tetrads.
Formalism: frame metric, inverse frame metric, null vectors l and n from T +/- X, complex null m from Y + iZ, and the tetrad decomposition of g_ab and g^ab.

Construction: write the Schwarzschild inverse metric in advanced EF coordinates as a null tetrad, complexify r, apply v -> v + i a cos(theta), r -> r + i a cos(theta), and demand reality to get the Kerr tetrad.
Catalogue: present the resulting advanced EF line element, transform to Boyer-Lindquist, and quote Kerr's original Cartesian form as flat metric minus a null-vector square.

Interpretation: parameters m and a; stationarity and axisymmetry; discrete t,phi and t,a symmetries; dt dphi cross term compared with a rotating frame in flat space; r versus Euclidean R; asymptotic flatness; 1/R expansion suggesting J proportional to ma.

Singular structure: curvature invariant blows up at rho = 0, which is a ring; infinite-redshift surfaces S_+/- from g_00; horizons r_+/- from Delta = 0; three regions; ergosphere between r_+ and S_+ (Fig. 20.3 summary).

Light-cone structure: search for theta = const null geodesics, obtain the constraint between L and N, solve for principal outgoing/ingoing congruences, integrate to logarithms showing r = r_+ is a coordinate singularity.
Extension: pick coordinates in which the ingoing principal congruence becomes dt-bar = -dr, recovering the advanced EF form and the light-cone diagram (Fig. 20.4).
Stationary limit: photons forced to circle at fixed r, theta; counter-rotation becomes impossible inside S_+; spatial diagram of wavefronts (Fig. 20.5).

Global structure: maximal extensions by analogy with RN for a^2 < m^2 and a^2 = m^2 (Figs 20.6-20.7), negative r, timelike avoidable ring and closed timelike curves; super-extremal case as two sheets glued through the disc and a naked singularity (Figs 20.8-20.9); cosmic censorship.

Astrophysics: collapse of a rotating star, Kerr-Newman by the same trick, no-hair and final-state picture (Fig. 20.10), white holes as the time reverse, Penrose process and superradiance (Fig. 20.11).

Global mass: charge as a flux integral at infinity (Fig. 20.12), Komar mass by analogy with a Killing-vector current, normalization fixed by Schwarzschild, asymptotic Killing vectors, ADM mass and positive energy theorem.

Singularity theorems: history from Finkelstein to Penrose 1965 and Hawking-Penrose 1970, the three-ingredient pattern, energy and genericity conditions, and the caveat that incompleteness is not the same as infinite curvature.
Quantum coda: area theorem and thermodynamic analogy, entropy as lost information, Hawking temperature, pair-creation picture (Fig. 20.13), evaporation times and primordial black holes.
signature_moves: Obtains a hard exact solution by an explicitly advertised 'trick' (Newman-Janis) on a null tetrad, then immediately cross-checks by reducing to Schwarzschild when a -> 0.

Collects three coordinate forms of the same metric in one section and then chooses whichever form makes each property transparent (Boyer-Lindquist for symmetries and horizons, Kerr-Schild for asymptotics and the ring, advanced EF for extension).
Uses discrete symmetries (t -> -t with phi -> -phi, or with a -> -a) as physical evidence of spin without any dynamics.
Compares the Kerr dt dphi cross term with the cross term produced by transforming flat space to a rotating frame, while openly flagging that rigid rotation in relativity has not been treated.
Reuses the exact diagnostic recipe of earlier chapters: g_00 = 0 gives infinite redshift, g^11 = 0 gives a null r = const hypersurface, radial null congruences give adapted coordinates.
Derives principal null congruences by counting equations: four first-integral equations for three unknowns force an algebraic constraint that selects the congruences.
Characterizes the stationary limit operationally with a photon constrained to circle at fixed r and theta and asks when dphi/dt can be non-positive.
Draws global structure 'by analogy with Reissner-Nordstrom' rather than deriving Kruskal-like charts, leaning on Penrose diagrams already familiar from ch18-19.
Motivates a gravitational mass integral from electromagnetic Gauss's law and fixes the normalization constant by demanding the Schwarzschild answer.
Presents the singularity theorems as a template of three hypotheses (boundary/initial condition, curvature condition, causality condition) rather than proving any of them.
Ends heavy mathematics with humour and cartoons (vase and television set, civilization living off a black hole) to fix the physical message.

sections.title: Null tetrads
sections.summary: Explains why the chapter uses a shortcut to Kerr and introduces the frame formalism needed for it. A set of four independent vectors defines a frame metric by contraction with g_ab, whose inverse raises and lowers frame indices; the relation can be inverted to rebuild g_ab from the tetrad. Starting from an orthonormal tetrad, the combinations (T +/- X)/sqrt2 give two real null vectors with l.n = 1, and (Y +/- iZ)/sqrt2 give a complex conjugate pair of null vectors with m.m-bar = -1. The resulting null tetrad has an off-diagonal frame metric, and the spacetime metric becomes l n + n l - m m-bar - m-bar m.
key_moves: Define g_ij = g_ab e_i^a e_j^b and argue invertibility from linear independence plus non-degeneracy of g_ab.
Rotate the T-X pair by 45 degrees in the light-cone sense to obtain l and n, null and cross-normalized to 1 (Fig. 20.1).
Complexify the transverse pair Y, Z into m and m-bar, each null, with m.m-bar = -1.
Read off the null-tetrad frame metric (20.14) and hence the decompositions (20.15)-(20.16) of g_ab and g^ab.

sections.title: The Kerr solution from a complex transformation
sections.summary: Carries out the Newman-Janis construction. The inverse Schwarzschild metric in advanced Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates is written as a null tetrad with l along the r direction, n containing the 1 - 2m/r factor and m spanning the angular directions. Allowing r to be complex, the tetrad is rewritten with 1/r replaced by the average of 1/r and 1/r-bar and with 1/r-bar in m, keeping l and n real. The formal shift v -> v + i a cos(theta), r -> r + i a cos(theta), followed by demanding the new v and r be real, produces a tetrad whose inverse metric is that of Kerr.
key_moves: List the nonzero contravariant components of Schwarzschild in advanced EF coordinates (20.17).
Factor g^ab into the tetrad (20.18) using (20.16).
Complexify r in a specific, non-unique way (20.19): real parts in l and n, conjugate r in m.
Apply the complex shift (20.20) and impose reality of v' and r' to obtain the Kerr tetrad (20.21), which picks up a -i a sin(theta) component along the v and r directions.

sections.title: The three main forms of the Kerr solution
sections.summary: Assembles the line element produced by the trick, in advanced EF form with functions rho^2 = r^2 + a^2 cos^2(theta). A transformation written in differentials (introducing Delta = r^2 - 2mr + a^2) converts it to the Boyer-Lindquist form, which is the Kerr analogue of Schwarzschild coordinates. Kerr's own Cartesian-type form is also quoted; it has the structure flat metric minus lambda times the square of a covector that is null in the flat metric, which is how Kerr originally found the solution, and it reduces to lambda = 2m/r with a radial null covector for Schwarzschild.
key_moves: Present (20.22) with rho^2 (20.23) and rename phi to phi-bar in anticipation of the later coordinate change.
Give the transformation to Boyer-Lindquist coordinates as differential relations (20.24)-(20.25), promising the explanation in §20.7.
Write Boyer-Lindquist (20.27) as two perfect squares in (dt - a sin^2 theta dphi) and ((r^2+a^2) dphi - a dt).
Quote the Kerr form (20.28) with Cartesian-type coordinates (20.29) and abstract it to the Kerr-Schild structure (20.30)-(20.31).

sections.title: Basic properties of the Kerr solution
sections.summary: Uses the Boyer-Lindquist form to argue that Kerr is a stationary, axisymmetric field of a spinning mass. Setting a = 0 gives Schwarzschild, identifying m. Independence of t and phi gives two Killing vectors; the metric is invariant under simultaneous reversal of t and phi (or t and a) but not under either alone, as expected for a spinning body. The single dt dphi cross term is compared with the cross term that appears when flat space is written in a uniformly rotating frame. The Boyer-Lindquist r is shown to differ from the Euclidean radius R except asymptotically; the metric approaches Minkowski at large R, and expanding in 1/R shows an off-diagonal g_0alpha term proportional to ma, suggesting angular momentum ma, supported by Lense-Thirring and multipole-moment arguments.
key_moves: Read off Killing vectors d/dt and d/dphi and the circular orbits of d/dphi.
Note invariance under (t, phi) -> (-t, -phi) and (t, a) -> (-t, -a): time reversal of a spinning body equals reversing its spin.
Transform flat space in cylindrical coordinates to a rotating frame (20.37)-(20.39) and exhibit the resulting dphi' dt term, with a disclaimer about rigid rotation.
Compute R^2 = r^2 + a^2 sin^2 theta from the Kerr form and expand for r >> a (20.41)-(20.42).
Expand (20.28) in 1/R (20.43) to see the mass term and a rotation term proportional to ma.

sections.title: Singularities and horizons
sections.summary: Locates the genuine singularity where the curvature invariant R^abcd R_abcd diverges, rho = 0, which in Kerr-form Cartesian coordinates is a ring of radius a in the equatorial plane. Infinite-redshift surfaces are taken where g_00 vanishes, giving two axisymmetric surfaces S_+/- that reduce to r = 2m and r = 0 for a = 0. The Killing vector d/dt is timelike outside S_+ and inside S_-, spacelike between. Horizons are found, as for Schwarzschild, where r = const surfaces become null, g^11 = -Delta/rho^2 = 0, giving r_+/- for a^2 < m^2, three regular regions, and an ergosphere between r_+ and S_+. A nine-point summary of Kerr properties closes the section.
key_moves: Solve rho^2 = 0 as r = 0 and theta = pi/2 and translate via (20.29) to x^2 + y^2 = a^2, z = 0.
Assert (without proof in stationary non-static case) that infinite redshift still occurs where g_00 = 0 and solve for r_{S+/-} (20.46).
Evaluate the norm of the time-translation Killing vector as g_00 to classify where it is timelike, null or spacelike.
Compute g^11 = -Delta/rho^2 and set Delta = 0 for the horizons (20.47); compare with S_+/- and note they touch only on the axis.

sections.title: The principal null congruences
sections.summary: Since rotation drags light, there are no radial null geodesics; the analogue is a pair of congruences at constant theta. Using the Boyer-Lindquist Lagrangian, the ignorable t and phi give first integrals L and N, the null condition gives a third, and the theta Euler-Lagrange equation with theta fixed gives a fourth. Four equations in three unknown velocities force the constraint (N + aL sin^2 theta)(N - aL sin^2 theta) = 0; choosing one factor yields t-dot, r-dot = +/- L, phi-dot, so r is an affine parameter. Integrating dt/dr and dphi/dr gives logarithms diverging at r_+/-, identifying the outgoing and ingoing principal congruences and signalling that r = r_+ is a coordinate singularity of Boyer-Lindquist coordinates.
key_moves: Argue from the non-removability of rotation that Kerr cannot be transformed into Schwarzschild, so radial null lines do not exist.
Write first integrals (20.49)-(20.50), the null condition (20.51) and the theta equation (20.52).
Use equation counting to derive the constraint (20.53) and restrict to (20.54).
Solve (20.55)-(20.57) and integrate (20.58)-(20.59) by partial fractions over r_+ and r_- to (20.60)-(20.61).
Use the sign of Delta in regions I, II, III to identify outgoing behaviour and obtain the ingoing congruence by t -> -t, phi -> -phi.

sections.title: Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
sections.summary: Mirrors the Schwarzschild construction: find new coordinates (t-bar, r, theta, phi-bar) in which the ingoing principal congruence is simply dt-bar = -dr at fixed angles. The needed shifts are dt-bar = dt + (2mr/Delta) dr and dphi-bar = dphi + (a/Delta) dr, and with advanced time v = t-bar + r the Boyer-Lindquist metric turns back into the advanced EF form produced by the Newman-Janis trick, which is regular through r_+. The corresponding two-dimensional spacetime diagram (Fig. 20.4) is compared with Reissner-Nordstrom.
key_moves: Write the ingoing congruence differentially (20.62)-(20.63) and state the target form (20.65).
Choose the transformation (20.66)-(20.67) that cancels the dr parts along the congruence.
Define v = t-bar + r (20.68) and recognize the result as (20.22), closing the loop opened in §20.3.

sections.title: The stationary limit
sections.summary: Considers the non-geodesic null curves with dr = dtheta = 0 in region I, representing light forced to circle at fixed r and theta. Solving the Boyer-Lindquist null condition gives two values of dphi/dt; the co-rotating one is always positive, and the counter-rotating one is non-positive only outside S_+ and vanishes on it. Hence on S_+ even light aimed against the rotation cannot move relative to infinity, and inside the ergosphere everything must co-rotate. This justifies calling S_+ the stationary limit surface; it is timelike (so crossable in both directions) except at the poles where it is null and touches the horizon. The equatorial spatial diagram (Fig. 20.5) shows the tipping of wavefronts.
key_moves: Impose dr = dtheta = ds^2 = 0 and solve the quadratic for dphi/dt (20.70).
Show the denominator of the minus-branch is positive for r > r_+.
Reduce dphi/dt <= 0 to Delta^{1/2} >= a sin theta, i.e. r >= r_{S+} (20.71).
Interpret: on S_+ a counter-rotating photon is momentarily stationary; inside it is swept forward.

sections.title: Maximal extension for the case a^2 < m^2
sections.summary: Describes, without full derivation, how advanced and retarded EF-type coordinates are patched together as for Reissner-Nordstrom to build the maximal analytic extension. The new feature is that r can be continued through the ring to negative values. Along the symmetry axis the conformal diagram (Fig. 20.6) is an infinite chain: stationary asymptotically flat regions I, non-stationary regions II where every point lies on a trapped surface, and regions III containing a timelike (hence avoidable) ring singularity and closed timelike curves. For a^2 = m^2 the horizons merge, regions II disappear, and the diagram resembles extreme RN (Fig. 20.7).
key_moves: Introduce u_+/- and phi_+/- (advanced and retarded) and combine charts as in ch19.
Restrict the conformal picture to the axis where horizons and infinite-redshift surfaces coincide.
Classify regions I, II, III by stationarity, trapping and causality violation.
Take the limit a^2 = m^2 to remove regions II.

sections.title: Maximal extension for the case a^2 > m^2
sections.summary: With a^2 > m^2, Delta never vanishes, so there are no horizons, only the ring. On a t = const slice the r = const surfaces are confocal ellipsoids that flatten to the disc bounded by the ring at r = 0. Continuing r to negative values through the disc means gluing the top of the disc to the bottom of a copy in a second sheet and vice versa (Fig. 20.8); passing through twice returns you. The negative-r sheet is asymptotically flat with negative mass. Near the ring d/dphi is timelike, giving closed timelike curves that can be deformed through any point, so causality fails badly. Only equatorial causal geodesics from the positive-r side hit the ring, but signals from it can spiral out (Fig. 20.9): a naked singularity, which motivates Penrose's cosmic censorship hypothesis.
key_moves: Invert (20.29) as a quartic for r in terms of x, y, z and identify confocal ellipsoids degenerating to the disc.
Construct the two-sheeted extension by identifying opposite faces of the disc.
Show d/dphi becomes timelike near the ring, producing closed timelike curves.
Observe the absence of horizons makes the ring visible from infinity and state cosmic censorship.

sections.title: Rotating black holes
sections.summary: Imagines a rotating star with Kerr exterior collapsing: observers cross r_+ and then r_-, but unlike Schwarzschild the collapse may halt and the extension suggests emergence into a new asymptotic region (no realistic interior solution is known; a toroidal source is speculated). Applying the Newman-Janis trick to Reissner-Nordstrom gives the Kerr-Newman solution with mass, spin and charge, its stationary limit surface and outer horizon for a^2 + epsilon^2 <= m^2. Realistic collapse radiates away asymmetries once a horizon forms and settles to Kerr-Newman: the no-hair picture (Fig. 20.10), whose time reverse is a white hole spitting out objects. Penrose's process of splitting a particle in the ergosphere so that one fragment escapes with more energy than was sent in, at the cost of the hole's spin, is described (Fig. 20.11), together with its link to superradiance and Zel'dovich's suggestion.
concepts: gravitational collapse to a rotating black hole
key_moves: Contrast the collapse sequence with Schwarzschild: halting inside r_- is allowed.
Reapply the complex trick to the RN seed to get (20.72) and its surfaces (20.73)-(20.74).
State the asymptotic uniqueness result and the dynamical picture of a trapped surface forming inside an expanding, then settling, event horizon.
Describe energy extraction in the ergosphere and trace the energy budget to the hole's angular momentum.

sections.title: The definition of mass in general relativity
sections.summary: Since general relativity has no local gravitational energy density, mass is defined for isolated systems by surface integrals at infinity. Electromagnetism motivates the construction: with the sourced Maxwell equation, total charge in a volume on a spacelike hypersurface becomes, by the divergence theorem, a flux of F^ab through its boundary, which gives q for a point charge. Replacing the current by R^ab K_b for a timelike Killing vector K and using the Killing identity turns the volume integral into a boundary integral of the derivative of K; with factor 1/4pi this Komar integral gives m for Schwarzschild. Because only the boundary is used, K need only be an asymptotic Killing vector. The ADM mass, an alternative from the Hamiltonian formulation, agrees for time-independent perturbations, and the Schoen-Yau positive energy theorem guarantees non-negative ADM mass under the dominant energy condition.
key_moves: Write the sourced Maxwell equation (20.75) and total charge as a volume integral over V (20.76), convert to a surface flux (20.78), and push the surface to infinity (20.79).
Evaluate with the Minkowski asymptotic metric to get (20.81) and check with a point charge (20.82).
Define J^a = R^ab K_b and E_total (20.83)-(20.84); use (20.85) to write J as a divergence and apply the divergence theorem (20.86).
For Schwarzschild compute unit normals (20.87)-(20.88), reduce the integrand to a Christoffel symbol (20.89), and integrate to m (20.90).
Generalize to asymptotic Killing vectors (20.91) and quote the ADM boundary integral (20.92).

sections.title: The singularity theorems
sections.summary: Recounts how singularities went from being dismissed as artefacts of symmetry (Schwarzschild 1916, Finkelstein 1958) to being expected generically after Penrose's 1965 theorem introduced trapped surfaces and geodesic incompleteness as the definition of a singular spacetime, followed by Hawking's cosmological version and the work of Hawking, Penrose, Ellis, Geroch and others. The general pattern: an initial/boundary condition, a curvature condition and a causality condition imply incomplete causal geodesics. For the 1970 Hawking-Penrose theorem these are a trapped surface, no closed timelike curves, and the timelike convergence condition, which via the Einstein equations becomes the strong energy condition; null versions use the null convergence condition implied by the weak energy condition; a genericity condition is also needed. The theorems predict incompleteness in models near Kerr-Newman collapse, Friedmann big bang/crunch and colliding plane waves, but do not establish curvature blow-up or the form of generic singularities.
key_moves: Define a singular spacetime by an inextendible causal geodesic of finite affine length.
State the three-part template of a pattern singularity theorem.
Translate the curvature condition (20.93) into matter terms (20.94)-(20.95) and the null version (20.96)-(20.97).
Add the genericity condition and discuss what the theorems do not claim.

sections.title: Black hole thermodynamics and Hawking radiation
sections.summary: A brief excursion beyond classical relativity. Horizon area grows when matter falls in and when holes merge, suggesting an analogy with entropy; Hawking and collaborators found analogues of the laws of thermodynamics, with the first law linking changes of mass and area through the surface gravity, which is uniform over the horizon like equilibrium temperature. Entropy is linked to the finite (by the uncertainty principle) number of possible progenitor configurations lost in collapse; finite entropy implies a finite temperature, which conflicts with a classical perfect absorber until Hawking showed that black holes emit thermal radiation with temperature inversely proportional to mass. A virtual-pair picture with one member falling in, reinterpreted as backward-in-time tunnelling (Fig. 20.13), explains the emission, which needs no rotation. Evaporation accelerates as mass drops; solar-mass holes last about 10^67 years, while primordial mini holes could be exploding now, though gamma-ray searches are inconclusive.
key_moves: Motivate area-entropy from monotonic growth under accretion and merger.
Link entropy to information loss via no-hair and count of configurations.
Resolve the equilibrium paradox by Hawking emission and quote T (20.98) with a numerical scale.
Give a heuristic pair-creation/tunnelling picture and derive the runaway nature of evaporation.

concepts.name: frame formalism
concepts.definition: Describing tensors by their components along a chosen set of four linearly independent vector fields e_i^a (a tetrad) rather than along coordinate basis vectors, with frame indices i, j raised and lowered by the frame metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from the orthonormal tetrad of §10.5 and generalized to arbitrary independent vector fields as preparation for null tetrads.
concepts.notes: The book only defines the frame metric; no frame connection coefficients or spin coefficients are introduced.

concepts.name: frame metric
concepts.definition: The 4x4 matrix of scalars g_ij = g_ab e_i^a e_j^b formed from the inner products of tetrad vectors; it is invertible (inverse g^ij) and lets the metric be rebuilt as g_ab = g_ij e^i_a e^j_b.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined at a point from four independent vectors; invertibility is argued from independence and non-degeneracy of g_ab.

concepts.name: null tetrad
concepts.definition: A tetrad (l^a, n^a, m^a, m-bar^a) of two real future-pointing null vectors with l.n = 1 and a complex conjugate pair of null vectors orthogonal to them with m.m-bar = -1 (in signature +---), so that g_ab = l_a n_b + n_a l_b - m_a m-bar_b - m-bar_a m_b.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from an orthonormal tetrad by taking (T +/- X)/sqrt2 and (Y +/- iZ)/sqrt2, with a sketch of l and n as the two light-cone directions in the T-X plane (Fig. 20.1).

concepts.name: complex null vector
concepts.definition: A complex vector m^a = (Y^a + i Z^a)/sqrt2 built from two orthogonal unit spacelike vectors; it satisfies m.m = 0 even though it is not a real light-like direction, and its conjugate completes the null tetrad.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as an 'advantageous' complexification of the transverse spatial pair so that all four tetrad legs are null.

concepts.name: Newman-Penrose formalism
concepts.definition: A version of the frame formalism in which all components are taken along a null tetrad, widely used in gravitational radiation and exact-solution work.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the systematic framework behind null tetrads; only the tetrad definition is developed here.

concepts.name: Newman-Janis algorithm
concepts.definition: A solution-generating heuristic: write a static seed metric's inverse as a null tetrad in advanced null coordinates, allow r to be complex with a prescribed placement of r and r-bar, perform the complex shift v -> v + i a cos(theta), r -> r + i a cos(theta), and require the new v and r to be real; applied to Schwarzschild it yields Kerr, and to Reissner-Nordstrom it yields Kerr-Newman.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as a shortcut avoiding a lengthy direct integration of the vacuum field equations; executed step by step on the Schwarzschild tetrad in advanced EF coordinates and later reused on RN.
concepts.notes: The book calls it a trick and offers no explanation of why it works; the complexification step is not unique and the method is not a general theorem.

concepts.name: Kerr solution
concepts.definition: The two-parameter (mass m, specific angular momentum a) stationary, axisymmetric, asymptotically flat vacuum solution of Einstein's equations describing the exterior of a rotating black hole; it reduces to Schwarzschild when a = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from Schwarzschild by the Newman-Janis trick, displayed in three coordinate forms, then interrogated with the same diagnostics used for Schwarzschild and RN.
concepts.notes: A nine-item property summary is given at the end of §20.5.

concepts.name: Boyer-Lindquist coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates (t, r, theta, phi) in which the Kerr metric is independent of t and phi, has a single off-diagonal dt dphi term, and reduces to Schwarzschild coordinates at a = 0; they are singular where Delta = r^2 - 2mr + a^2 vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached from the advanced EF form by differential relations dv = dt + (r^2 + a^2)/Delta dr and dphi-bar = dphi + a/Delta dr, whose origin is explained in §20.7.

concepts.name: Kerr-Schild form
concepts.definition: A way of writing a metric as the Minkowski metric minus lambda times the square of a covector l_a that is null with respect to the Minkowski metric; Kerr's original Cartesian-type form of his solution has this structure, with Schwarzschild as the case lambda = 2m/r, l_a = (1, x/r, y/r, z/r).
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as Kerr's original discovery form, then abstracted to the general structure and specialized back to Schwarzschild.
concepts.notes: The book calls it the 'Kerr form'; the standard name Kerr-Schild is not used. The printed components (20.33) have a^2 + y^2 in the denominators where a^2 + r^2 is meant.

concepts.name: advanced Eddington-Finkelstein form of Kerr
concepts.definition: The Kerr metric written in coordinates (v, r, theta, phi-bar) adapted to the ingoing principal null congruence, in which the metric is regular across the outer horizon r = r_+.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears first as the direct output of the Newman-Janis trick (§20.3) and is then re-derived in §20.7 as the coordinate system in which ingoing principal null geodesics become lines of constant v at fixed theta and phi-bar.

concepts.name: Kerr spin parameter
concepts.definition: The parameter a in the Kerr metric, equal to the angular momentum per unit mass J/m (dimension of length in geometrized units); J = ma is the angular momentum measured at infinity and the sign of a gives the sense of rotation.
concepts.how_introduced: Inferred from three suggestive arguments: invariance under (t, a) -> (-t, -a), comparison with Lense-Thirring and multipole moments, and the ma coefficient in the 1/R expansion of g_0alpha.
concepts.notes: The text says a is 'related to the angular velocity'; strictly it is angular momentum per unit mass, not an angular velocity.

concepts.name: stationary spacetime
concepts.definition: A spacetime admitting a Killing vector field that is timelike (at least in an asymptotic region), so the geometry does not change along its orbits; unlike a static spacetime it may contain time-space cross terms that cannot be removed.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from t-independence of the Boyer-Lindquist metric, with the caveat that d/dt is timelike only outside S_+.

concepts.name: axisymmetric spacetime
concepts.definition: A spacetime with a Killing vector field (here d/dphi) whose orbits are closed circles about an invariantly defined axis, so the geometry is unchanged under rotations about that axis.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from phi-independence of the Boyer-Lindquist metric; the orbits t, r, theta = const are identified as circles.

concepts.name: discrete t-phi reflection symmetry
concepts.definition: The Kerr metric is unchanged by reversing t and phi together (or t and a together) but not by reversing either alone, which is the symmetry expected of the field of a spinning body.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the first physical clue that Kerr describes rotation: running a spinning object backward in time looks like the same object spinning the other way.

concepts.name: frame dragging
concepts.definition: The effect of a rotating mass on local inertial frames and light cones: near the source, freely falling frames and light are forced to rotate with it, signalled in the metric by an irremovable dt dphi term and culminating in compulsory co-rotation inside the ergosphere.
concepts.how_introduced: Suggested by the dt dphi cross term compared with a flat metric in a rotating frame (§20.4), invoked to explain the absence of radial null geodesics (§20.6), and made operational at the stationary limit (§20.8).
concepts.notes: The term 'frame dragging' is used only loosely ('drag space around with it'); the book stresses that rotation cannot be transformed away, unlike in Newtonian theory.

concepts.name: Lense-Thirring effect
concepts.definition: The weak-field gravitomagnetic field outside a slowly rotating body, which drags inertial frames and whose off-diagonal metric terms are fixed by the body's angular momentum.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as one independent argument identifying ma with the Kerr angular momentum.

concepts.name: Boyer-Lindquist radial coordinate
concepts.definition: The Kerr coordinate r is not the Euclidean distance: with Kerr-form Cartesian coordinates, R^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = r^2 + a^2 sin^2 theta, so r = const surfaces are confocal oblate spheroids that coincide with spheres only asymptotically or when a = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown by computing R from the Kerr-form coordinate relations and expanding for r >> a; later used to see r = 0 as a disc and to extend r negative.
concepts.notes: When the book gives S_+ a 'radius' 2m at the equator and m + (m^2 - a^2)^{1/2} at the poles, these are values of the coordinate r, not Euclidean or proper radii; worth flagging given this very point.

concepts.name: asymptotic flatness
concepts.definition: The metric approaches the Minkowski metric (in suitable coordinates) at large distance from the source, so that spacetime looks flat far away and quantities like total mass can be defined at infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Checked for Kerr by letting R -> infinity in the Kerr form; used again as the setting for Komar and ADM mass.

concepts.name: ring singularity
concepts.definition: The curvature singularity of Kerr at rho^2 = r^2 + a^2 cos^2 theta = 0, i.e. r = 0 on the equator, which in Kerr-form Cartesian coordinates is a ring x^2 + y^2 = a^2 in the plane z = 0; it is timelike and can be avoided, and one can pass through the disc it bounds into a negative-r region.
concepts.how_introduced: Found from divergence of the invariant R^abcd R_abcd at rho = 0 and translated into Cartesian terms; described as surprising.

concepts.name: Kretschmann scalar
concepts.definition: The curvature invariant formed by fully contracting the Riemann tensor with itself; its divergence signals a genuine curvature singularity independent of coordinates.
concepts.how_introduced: Used without computation to certify that rho = 0 is intrinsic.

concepts.name: infinite-redshift surface
concepts.definition: A hypersurface on which light emitted by an observer at rest relative to infinity would arrive infinitely redshifted; in Kerr it lies where g_00 vanishes, giving S_+/-: r = m +/- (m^2 - a^2 cos^2 theta)^{1/2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken over from the static case by assertion ('it can be shown') and then linked to the norm of the time-translation Killing vector.

concepts.name: Kerr event horizons
concepts.definition: For a^2 < m^2, the null hypersurfaces r = r_+/- = m +/- (m^2 - a^2)^{1/2} where Delta = 0; r_+ is the event horizon of the black hole and r_- an inner (Cauchy-type) horizon; together they split Boyer-Lindquist r > 0 into regions I, II, III.
concepts.how_introduced: Found, as for Schwarzschild, by asking where r = const surfaces become null, i.e. where g^11 = -Delta/rho^2 vanishes.
concepts.notes: The g^11 = 0 criterion locates null r = const surfaces; the book does not use Killing horizons or discuss that the horizon generator is a combination of d/dt and d/dphi.

concepts.name: ergosphere
concepts.definition: The region between the outer event horizon r_+ and the stationary limit surface S_+, outside the black hole, where the time-translation Killing vector is spacelike so that no observer can remain at rest relative to infinity and everything is forced to co-rotate; negative-energy states exist there, enabling the Penrose process.
concepts.how_introduced: Named when comparing S_+ with r_+ (they touch only on the axis), shaded in Fig. 20.3, made operational by the photon-orbit argument of §20.8, and exploited in §20.11.

concepts.name: stationary limit surface
concepts.definition: The outer infinite-redshift surface S_+ of Kerr: the boundary inside which no timelike or null curve can keep fixed r, theta, phi, because even a photon aimed against the rotation has dphi/dt >= 0 there; it is timelike except at the poles, so it can be crossed both inward and outward.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by considering photons forced to orbit at fixed r and theta and finding where the counter-rotating solution for dphi/dt reaches zero.

concepts.name: principal null congruences
aliases: principal congruences of outgoing and ingoing null geodesics
concepts.definition: The two families of null geodesics in Kerr at fixed theta with r-dot = +/- L, t-dot = (r^2 + a^2)L/Delta, phi-dot = aL/Delta; they are the most outgoing and most ingoing light rays at each point and play the role of radial null geodesics in Schwarzschild.
concepts.how_introduced: Found by imposing theta = const on the Boyer-Lindquist geodesic equations, using first integrals and a four-equations-three-unknowns constraint.
concepts.notes: Geometrically they are the repeated principal null directions of the Weyl tensor (Kerr is Petrov type D), a point the book does not make.

concepts.name: affine parameter
concepts.definition: A parameter along a geodesic for which the geodesic equation takes its standard form; here r itself is affine along the principal congruences because r-dot is constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Noted in passing after solving r-dot = +/- L.

concepts.name: coordinate singularity
concepts.definition: A place where a metric's components blow up or degenerate because of a bad choice of coordinates, not because curvature diverges; it can be removed by a coordinate change.
concepts.how_introduced: Recognized at r = r_+ because t and phi along the principal congruences diverge logarithmically while curvature is finite, then removed with EF-type coordinates.

concepts.name: static observer
concepts.definition: An observer whose world line follows the time-translation Killing vector, staying at fixed spatial Boyer-Lindquist coordinates; such observers exist only where that Killing vector is timelike, i.e. outside S_+.
concepts.how_introduced: Implicit in the photon-orbit analysis: on S_+ a counter-rotating photon is only just stationary, so massive observers cannot be.

concepts.name: maximal analytic extension of Kerr
concepts.definition: The largest spacetime obtained by patching together Eddington-Finkelstein-type charts (advanced and retarded) across the Kerr horizons and continuing r through the ring to negative values; for a^2 < m^2 it is an infinite chain of regions I, II, III as seen on the axis.
concepts.how_introduced: Described by analogy with Reissner-Nordstrom rather than constructed explicitly; displayed as axis Penrose diagrams.

concepts.name: Penrose diagram
concepts.definition: A conformally compactified spacetime diagram in which light rays run at 45 degrees and infinity is brought to finite boundaries (scri-plus, scri-minus), showing causal structure of an entire spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Used, drawn along the symmetry axis only, for the Kerr extensions in the sub-extremal and extremal cases.

concepts.name: trapped surface
concepts.definition: A closed spacelike 2-surface so deep in a gravitational field that both outgoing and ingoing future-directed light rays orthogonal to it converge.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from §18.5 to characterize Kerr regions II; reintroduced in §20.13 as the boundary condition of Penrose-type singularity theorems.

concepts.name: closed timelike curves
concepts.definition: Future-directed timelike curves that return to their starting event, allowing an observer to meet their own past; in Kerr they occur near the ring on the negative-r side, where d/dphi is timelike so circles of constant t, r, theta are timelike.
concepts.how_introduced: Pointed out in regions III of the sub-extremal extension and shown explicitly for a^2 > m^2, where they can be deformed through any point.

concepts.name: extremal Kerr black hole
concepts.definition: The Kerr solution with a^2 = m^2, in which the inner and outer horizons coincide at r = m and the non-stationary regions II disappear; its conformal structure resembles extreme Reissner-Nordstrom.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken as a limit in §20.9 with a Penrose diagram along the axis.

concepts.name: negative-r region
concepts.definition: The part of the maximally extended Kerr spacetime reached by passing through the disc bounded by the ring singularity, where r < 0; it is asymptotically flat at large negative r and there the field looks like that of a negative mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by analytic continuation of r through the disc, visualized as identifying the top of one disc with the bottom of another in a second copy of space.

concepts.name: super-extremal Kerr
concepts.definition: The Kerr solution with a^2 > m^2, where Delta > 0 everywhere so there are no horizons; the ring singularity is exposed, the extension through the disc is two-sheeted, and closed timelike curves pervade it.
concepts.how_introduced: Treated in its own section as the case where the Boyer-Lindquist metric is regular except at the ring.

concepts.name: naked singularity
concepts.definition: A spacetime singularity not hidden behind an event horizon, so that causal signals from it can reach distant observers.
concepts.how_introduced: Illustrated by a light signal spiralling out from the ring of super-extremal Kerr (Fig. 20.9).

concepts.name: cosmic censorship hypothesis
concepts.definition: Penrose's conjecture that physically reasonable evolution does not produce naked singularities, so singularities are always hidden inside event horizons; several inequivalent mathematical formulations exist and it remains an open research problem.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as a way to exclude the 'wild speculation' naked singularities would permit.

concepts.name: geodesic incompleteness
concepts.definition: A spacetime is singular if some timelike or null geodesic cannot be extended beyond a finite proper time or affine parameter, and the spacetime cannot be extended to continue it.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the modern criterion introduced in Penrose's 1965 paper; used for the ring in §20.10 and as the conclusion of singularity theorems.

concepts.name: Kerr-Newman solution
concepts.definition: The stationary axisymmetric electrovacuum solution with mass m, spin parameter a and charge epsilon; it has a stationary limit surface r = m + (m^2 - epsilon^2 - a^2 cos^2 theta)^{1/2} and, if a^2 + epsilon^2 <= m^2, an outer horizon r = m + (m^2 - epsilon^2 - a^2)^{1/2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained (as an exercise) by applying the Newman-Janis trick to Reissner-Nordstrom in advanced EF coordinates; presented as the most general black hole.

concepts.name: no-hair theorem
aliases: a black hole has no hair
concepts.definition: The collection of uniqueness results implying that a stationary black hole in asymptotically flat Einstein-Maxwell theory is described by Kerr-Newman, fixed entirely by mass, angular momentum and charge, so all other details of the collapsed matter are lost.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a theorem that the exterior of a forming horizon approaches Kerr-Newman, then dramatized by Wheeler's picture of a vase and a television falling in.
concepts.notes: The rigorous theorems (Israel, Carter, Robinson, Mazur, Bunting) concern stationary black holes; that collapse dynamically settles to Kerr-Newman is a strongly supported but more delicate claim than the text suggests.

concepts.name: gravitational collapse to a rotating black hole
concepts.definition: The process in which a rotating body collapses inside its horizon; asymmetries are radiated away as a trapped surface forms inside a still-expanding event horizon that then settles to a stationary Kerr(-Newman) hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Told as an idealized collapse through r_+ and r_- (with possible halting and re-emergence in the extension) and then as the realistic settling picture.
concepts.notes: No physically realistic interior Kerr solution is known; the text speculates a toroidal source.

concepts.name: white hole
concepts.definition: The time reverse of a black hole: a region out of which matter and light emerge and which nothing can enter.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned humorously as the time reversal of the no-hair cartoon.

concepts.name: Penrose process
aliases: energy extraction from a rotating black hole
concepts.definition: A mechanism in which a particle entering the ergosphere splits so that one fragment falls into the hole on a negative-energy orbit while the other escapes with more energy than the original, the difference being paid for by a reduction of the hole's angular momentum and mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Described qualitatively, with a fanciful engineering cartoon of a civilization living off the hole (Fig. 20.11).
concepts.notes: No calculation or efficiency figure is given; negative-energy orbits are not explained.

concepts.name: superradiance
concepts.definition: Amplification of waves scattered off a rotating body when the wave's angular phase velocity is below the body's rotation rate, extracting rotational energy; the wave analogue of the Penrose process.
concepts.how_introduced: Linked to the Penrose process through Zel'dovich's 1971 suggestion from spinning metal spheres; used as a bridge to Hawking radiation.

concepts.name: Gauss-law charge integral
aliases: total charge as a surface integral
concepts.definition: Using the sourced Maxwell equation and the divergence theorem to express the charge inside a region of a spacelike hypersurface as the flux of F^ab through its boundary 2-surface, and total charge as that flux through a sphere at infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as a warm-up and template for defining gravitational mass, checked on a point charge.

concepts.name: Eulerian observer
concepts.definition: An observer whose 4-velocity is the unit timelike normal n^a to a spacelike hypersurface in a 3+1 split.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from ch14 to interpret j^a n_a as measured charge density.

concepts.name: Killing vector Ricci identity
concepts.definition: For any Killing vector K^a, the divergence of its covariant derivative is governed by the Ricci tensor: nabla_a nabla_b K^a = R_ab K^a (sign depending on curvature conventions).
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from Exercise 7.14 to rewrite the gravitational 'current' R^ab K_b as a divergence.

concepts.name: Komar mass
concepts.definition: The total mass-energy of a stationary (or asymptotically stationary) asymptotically flat spacetime defined as (1/4pi) times the flux of the antisymmetric tensor nabla^a K^b through a 2-sphere at infinity, where K is the timelike (asymptotic) Killing vector; it gives m for Schwarzschild.
concepts.how_introduced: Built by analogy with charge: replace j^a by R^ab K_b, integrate over a hypersurface, convert to a boundary term with the Killing identity, and fix the 1/4pi by matching Schwarzschild.
concepts.notes: Sign bookkeeping in (20.89)-(20.90) is glossed; see gaps.

concepts.name: asymptotic Killing vector
concepts.definition: A vector field that approaches a Killing vector of Minkowski space at infinity, even if it is not a Killing vector of the full spacetime; enough for defining conserved quantities by surface integrals at infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to extend the Komar construction from strictly stationary to asymptotically flat spacetimes.

concepts.name: ADM mass
concepts.definition: The total mass-energy of an asymptotically flat spacetime computed from the fall-off of the spatial metric perturbation h_ij on a spacelike slice as (1/16pi) times a flux integral of d_j h^j_i - d_i h^j_j at infinity; it arises from the boundary term of the ADM Hamiltonian.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as an alternative to Komar from the Hamiltonian viewpoint of §14.11, agreeing with Komar for time-independent h_ij.

concepts.name: positive energy theorem
concepts.definition: If the dominant energy condition holds, every asymptotically flat spacetime has non-negative ADM mass, and zero ADM mass only for Minkowski space (Schoen and Yau).
concepts.how_introduced: Stated without proof after the ADM mass.

concepts.name: singularity theorems
concepts.definition: Theorems showing that a spacetime obeying a suitable initial or boundary condition (e.g. a trapped surface), a curvature (energy) condition, and a causality condition must contain inextendible incomplete causal geodesics.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented historically and then as Senovilla's three-ingredient template, with the Hawking-Penrose 1970 theorem as the worked instance.
concepts.notes: The book balances the theorems by noting that many exact solutions are geodesically complete (maximal and singularity-free); the theorems bite for models close to Kerr-Newman collapse, Friedmann big bang/crunch, or colliding plane waves, and say nothing definite about the structure of generic singularities.

concepts.name: Hawking-Penrose singularity theorem
concepts.definition: The 1970 theorem that a spacetime with a closed trapped surface (or analogous condition), the timelike convergence condition, the generic condition and no closed timelike curves is causal-geodesically incomplete.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to instantiate each slot of the general template.

concepts.name: timelike convergence condition
concepts.definition: The requirement R_ab V^a V^b >= 0 for all non-spacelike V^a, which by Raychaudhuri's equation makes initially converging congruences of geodesics focus.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the curvature ingredient of the Hawking-Penrose theorem, then rephrased as the strong energy condition.

concepts.name: strong energy condition
concepts.definition: T_ab V^a V^b >= (1/2) T g_ab V^a V^b for all non-spacelike V^a; for matter with density mu and principal stresses p_alpha it means mu + p_alpha >= 0 and mu + sum p_alpha >= 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from the timelike convergence condition via the Einstein equations to give it a matter interpretation.
concepts.notes: Violated by a positive cosmological constant or inflationary scalar fields, a point not mentioned.

concepts.name: null convergence condition
concepts.definition: R_ab k^a k^b >= 0 for all null vectors k^a; it forces focusing of null geodesic congruences and underlies Penrose's 1965 theorem.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the null version of the convergence condition.

concepts.name: weak energy condition
concepts.definition: T^ab V_a V_b >= 0 for all non-spacelike V; for standard matter mu >= 0 and mu + p_alpha >= 0; it implies the null convergence condition.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the physical justification for the null convergence condition and compared with the dominant energy condition.

concepts.name: generic condition
concepts.definition: Every causal geodesic somewhere encounters curvature with a non-vanishing tidal component orthogonal to it, written as a non-zero antisymmetrized contraction of the Riemann tensor with the geodesic's tangent; it fails only in special, highly symmetric situations.
concepts.how_introduced: Added as a technical hypothesis of the Hawking-Penrose theorem.

concepts.name: Raychaudhuri focusing
concepts.definition: Given the convergence condition, a congruence of geodesics orthogonal to a hypersurface that starts to converge will converge ever faster and focus within finite affine parameter, provided the geodesics extend that far.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked by forward reference to (23.44) to explain why the curvature condition matters.

concepts.name: black hole area theorem
aliases: second law of black hole mechanics
concepts.definition: Classically (given the null energy condition), the area of an event horizon never decreases; it grows under accretion, and a merged hole has more area than the sum of its progenitors.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the observation that motivates the entropy analogy.
concepts.notes: Hawking evaporation violates the classical energy condition and does shrink the area; the text does not reconcile this.

concepts.name: black hole thermodynamics
concepts.definition: The exact correspondence between laws of black hole mechanics and thermodynamics: horizon area plays the role of entropy, surface gravity of temperature, and the first law relates mass change to area change weighted by surface gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced through the area-entropy resemblance and uniformity of surface gravity over the horizon.
formulas: \delta M=\frac{\kappa}{8\pi}\delta A+\Omega_H\delta J+\Phi_H\delta Q\;(\text{standard form, not in text})

concepts.name: surface gravity
concepts.definition: A measure of gravitational field strength at a Killing horizon (the force per unit mass needed at infinity to hold a unit mass at the horizon), constant over a stationary horizon; kappa = 1/(4m) for Schwarzschild.
concepts.how_introduced: Named, without a formula, as the proportionality factor in the first law and the analogue of temperature.

concepts.name: Bekenstein-Hawking entropy
concepts.definition: The entropy assigned to a black hole, proportional to its horizon area (S = k_B c^3 A / (4 G hbar)), interpreted as the logarithm of the number of internal configurations compatible with its mass, charge and spin.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated heuristically: no-hair means many possible progenitors, quantum mechanics makes the count finite, and its logarithm is the entropy.
concepts.notes: The area-entropy formula S = A/4 (geometric units) is not given in the text.

concepts.name: Hawking radiation
concepts.definition: Thermal emission of particles by any black hole due to quantum field effects near the horizon, with black-body temperature T = hbar c^3 / (8 pi G k_B M) for a Schwarzschild hole of mass M.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the resolution of the paradox that finite entropy implies finite temperature yet classical holes cannot emit; pictured as separation of virtual pairs with backward-in-time reinterpretation.

concepts.name: black hole evaporation
concepts.definition: The gradual loss of mass through Hawking radiation; since temperature rises as mass falls, emission runs away and the hole eventually disappears, over roughly 10^67 years for a solar mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Deduced qualitatively from the inverse mass-temperature relation.

concepts.name: primordial black holes
concepts.definition: Black holes hypothetically formed in the early universe, with masses small enough that they would be finishing their evaporation today, possibly as bursts of high-energy gamma rays.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the observationally interesting end of evaporation; searches reported inconclusive.

key_equations.name: Frame metric
key_equations.meaning: Inner products of the tetrad legs form a scalar matrix that plays the role of a metric on frame indices.
key_equations.symbols: e_i^a tetrad legs (i frame label, a tensor index); g_ab spacetime metric

key_equations.name: Inverse frame metric
key_equations.meaning: Defines the contravariant frame metric used to raise frame indices.
key_equations.symbols: g^ij inverse frame metric

key_equations.name: Metric from tetrad
key_equations.meaning: The spacetime metric is recovered from the tetrad and the frame metric; the null-tetrad version is (20.15).
key_equations.symbols: e^i_a dual tetrad (frame index raised with g^ij)

key_equations.name: Real null legs
key_equations.meaning: The two light-cone directions in the T-X plane of an orthonormal tetrad.
key_equations.symbols: T^a unit timelike; X^a, Y^a, Z^a unit spacelike, mutually orthogonal

key_equations.name: Null and normalization conditions for l, n
key_equations.meaning: l and n are null and cross-normalized.

key_equations.name: Frame metric for (l, n, Y, Z)
key_equations.meaning: Intermediate frame metric after replacing T, X by l, n.

key_equations.name: Complex null legs
key_equations.meaning: Complex null vectors spanning the 2-plane orthogonal to l and n.

key_equations.name: Conditions on m
key_equations.meaning: m is null and normalized against its conjugate.

key_equations.name: Null tetrad frame metric
key_equations.meaning: Frame metric of the null tetrad (l, n, m, m-bar); the export garbles the left-hand side as g_{g-bar}, the page shows g_ij.

key_equations.name: Null tetrad decomposition of the metric
key_equations.meaning: The metric is a sum of symmetrized products of null tetrad legs.

key_equations.name: Contravariant decomposition
key_equations.meaning: The form used to read off an inverse metric from a tetrad, the key tool of the Newman-Janis construction.

key_equations.name: Inverse Schwarzschild metric in advanced EF coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Seed metric for the complex trick, coordinates (v, r, theta, phi).
key_equations.symbols: x^0 = v advanced time, x^1 = r

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild null tetrad
key_equations.meaning: Tetrad reproducing (20.17) via (20.16).

key_equations.name: Complexified Schwarzschild tetrad
key_equations.meaning: The specific (non-unique) way of letting r be complex that keeps l and n real.
key_equations.symbols: r-bar complex conjugate of r

key_equations.name: Newman-Janis complex shift
key_equations.meaning: The formal complex coordinate transformation that introduces the rotation parameter a.
key_equations.symbols: a real parameter, later the spin

key_equations.name: Kerr null tetrad
key_equations.meaning: Result of the trick after requiring v', r' real; its inverse metric via (20.16) is Kerr.

key_equations.name: Kerr in advanced Eddington-Finkelstein form
key_equations.meaning: Kerr line element regular across the outer horizon, adapted to ingoing principal null geodesics.
key_equations.symbols: v advanced time; phi-bar shifted azimuth

key_equations.name: rho squared
key_equations.meaning: Ubiquitous Kerr function; its zero locates the ring singularity.

key_equations.name: Advanced EF to Boyer-Lindquist
key_equations.meaning: Differential coordinate change removing the dr cross terms.

key_equations.name: Delta
key_equations.meaning: Horizon function; Delta = 0 gives r_+/-.

key_equations.name: Kerr in Boyer-Lindquist form
key_equations.meaning: The standard stationary axisymmetric form, reducing to Schwarzschild coordinates at a = 0.
key_equations.symbols: m mass; a spin parameter

key_equations.name: Kerr's original Cartesian form
key_equations.meaning: Flat metric minus the square of a null one-form; makes asymptotic flatness and the ring manifest.
key_equations.symbols: r defined implicitly by (x, y, z)

key_equations.name: Kerr-form Cartesian coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Relates Cartesian-type coordinates to the spheroidal (r, theta, phi).

key_equations.name: Kerr-Schild structure
key_equations.meaning: General class of metrics Kerr searched within.
key_equations.symbols: lambda scalar function; l_a null in eta

key_equations.name: Kerr-Schild data for Kerr
key_equations.meaning: Explicit lambda and null covector; matches (20.28).
key_equations.symbols: Printed (20.33) has a^2 + y^2 in both denominators, a misprint for a^2 + r^2 (confirmed on the rendered page and by comparison with (20.28)).

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild in Kerr-Schild form
key_equations.meaning: a = 0 limit: flat metric minus 2m/r times a radial null square.

key_equations.name: Discrete symmetry
key_equations.meaning: Kerr is invariant under joint reversal of time and rotation sense, suggesting a spinning source.

key_equations.name: Newtonian rotating frame
key_equations.meaning: Transformation to a frame rotating with angular velocity a about z.
key_equations.symbols: a here is an angular velocity (reuse of the letter)

key_equations.name: Flat space in a rotating frame
key_equations.meaning: Rotation produces a dphi dt cross term, the analogue of the Kerr off-diagonal term.

key_equations.name: Euclidean radius versus Boyer-Lindquist r
key_equations.meaning: r differs from the flat radius except asymptotically or at a = 0.

key_equations.name: Large-R expansion of Kerr
key_equations.meaning: Mass appears in g_00 and angular momentum ma in the time-space cross term.
key_equations.symbols: Printed as (x dy - y dz); the second differential should be dx, as the axial rotation term requires.

key_equations.name: Ring singularity
key_equations.meaning: rho = 0 is a ring of radius a in the equatorial plane.

key_equations.name: g_00 in Boyer-Lindquist
key_equations.meaning: Norm of the time-translation Killing vector; its zeros are infinite-redshift surfaces.

key_equations.name: Infinite-redshift surfaces
key_equations.meaning: S_+ is the stationary limit surface; S_- lies inside the inner horizon.

key_equations.name: Radial inverse metric component
key_equations.meaning: r = const is null where this vanishes.

key_equations.name: Kerr horizons
key_equations.meaning: Outer (event) and inner horizons for a^2 < m^2; they merge at a^2 = m^2 and disappear for a^2 > m^2.

key_equations.name: Conditions for theta = const null geodesics
key_equations.meaning: Printed compactly as theta-dot = ds^2 = 0; the dot is derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

key_equations.name: First integrals from t and phi
key_equations.meaning: Conserved momenta conjugate to the ignorable coordinates t and phi (energy-like L and angular-momentum-like N).
key_equations.symbols: L, N constants

key_equations.name: Null condition
key_equations.meaning: The tangent vector is null.

key_equations.name: theta equation at fixed theta
key_equations.meaning: Consistency of staying at constant theta; the fourth equation for three unknown velocities.

key_equations.name: Constraint selecting the principal congruences
key_equations.meaning: Overdetermination forces a relation between the constants; one branch is chosen.

key_equations.name: Principal null congruence tangents
key_equations.meaning: Tangent components of the outgoing (+) and ingoing (-) principal null geodesics; r is affine.

key_equations.name: Congruence slopes
key_equations.meaning: Both diverge at Delta = 0, signalling the Boyer-Lindquist coordinate singularity.

key_equations.name: Outgoing congruence t(r)
key_equations.meaning: Kerr analogue of the Schwarzschild tortoise relation; logarithmic divergence at both horizons.

key_equations.name: Outgoing congruence phi(r)
key_equations.meaning: Light rays wind infinitely in phi as they approach a horizon in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates.

key_equations.name: Ingoing congruence in differential form
key_equations.meaning: Starting point for adapted coordinates.

key_equations.name: Target form of ingoing congruence
key_equations.meaning: Ingoing principal null lines become straight 45-degree lines at fixed angles.

key_equations.name: Kerr Eddington-Finkelstein transformation
key_equations.meaning: Maps Boyer-Lindquist to the advanced EF form (20.22).

key_equations.name: Constrained circular photon
key_equations.meaning: Null curves at fixed r and theta (not geodesics).

key_equations.name: Angular velocity of circling photons
key_equations.meaning: Co-rotating (+) and counter-rotating (-) angular velocities of light held at fixed r, theta.

key_equations.name: Stationary limit criterion
key_equations.meaning: Counter-rotation relative to infinity is possible only outside S_+.

key_equations.name: Advanced and retarded Kerr null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Charts combined to build the maximal extension.

key_equations.name: Kerr-form r in Cartesian terms
key_equations.meaning: Implicit definition of r; r = const are confocal ellipsoids degenerating to the disc at r = 0.

key_equations.name: Reissner-Nordstrom seed in advanced EF
key_equations.meaning: Seed for Kerr-Newman.
key_equations.symbols: Printed with dr^2 as the first differential; it must be dv^2 (compare (20.22) at a = 0).

key_equations.name: Kerr-Newman in advanced EF form
key_equations.meaning: Charged rotating black hole; label recovered from the rendered page (the export drops it).
key_equations.symbols: epsilon charge

key_equations.name: Kerr-Newman stationary limit and outer horizon
key_equations.meaning: Charge and spin both shrink the horizon; no horizon if a^2 + epsilon^2 > m^2.

key_equations.name: Sourced Maxwell equation
key_equations.meaning: Charges and currents source the field.
key_equations.symbols: j^a 4-current

key_equations.name: Charge as volume integral
key_equations.meaning: Charge density measured by Eulerian observers integrated over a region of a spacelike slice.
key_equations.symbols: n^a unit normal to Sigma; gamma det of induced 3-metric

key_equations.name: Charge as flux
key_equations.meaning: Divergence theorem turns enclosed charge into a boundary flux.
key_equations.symbols: m^b unit normal to U within Sigma; sigma det of induced 2-metric

key_equations.name: Total charge at infinity
key_equations.meaning: Charge depends only on the asymptotic field.
key_equations.symbols: S sphere at infinity

key_equations.name: Point charge check
key_equations.meaning: Lorentz-Heaviside point charge recovers q.

key_equations.name: Gravitational current and mass
key_equations.meaning: Analogy: Ricci tensor contracted with the timelike Killing vector plays the role of the charge current.
key_equations.symbols: K^a timelike Killing vector

key_equations.name: Killing identity
key_equations.meaning: Makes J^a a divergence so a boundary integral results.

key_equations.name: Komar mass as a surface integral
key_equations.meaning: Mass of a stationary spacetime as a flux of the Killing vector's derivative.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild unit normals
key_equations.meaning: Unit timelike normal to t = const and unit radial normal to spheres.
key_equations.symbols: The preceding normalization line prints (m^0)^2 where (m^1)^2 is meant.

key_equations.name: Reduction to a Christoffel symbol
key_equations.meaning: The integrand collapses to g_00 Gamma^0_01, whose magnitude is m/r^2.
key_equations.symbols: Direct evaluation gives -m/r^2; the text's 'simply m/r^2' drops the sign, which must be absorbed in the orientation of m^a or the sign convention of the definition.

key_equations.name: Komar mass of Schwarzschild
key_equations.meaning: Fixes the 1/4pi normalization.

key_equations.name: Komar mass (asymptotic)
key_equations.meaning: Defined with K only an asymptotic timelike Killing vector; label recovered from the rendered page.

key_equations.name: ADM mass
key_equations.meaning: Mass from spatial metric fall-off; equals Komar for time-independent h_ij. Label recovered from the rendered page.
key_equations.symbols: h_ab = g_ab - eta_ab

key_equations.name: Timelike convergence condition
key_equations.meaning: Curvature condition guaranteeing geodesic focusing.

key_equations.name: Strong energy condition
key_equations.meaning: Matter form of (20.93) via the field equations.

key_equations.name: Strong energy condition for standard matter
key_equations.meaning: Violated only by negative densities or large negative pressures.
key_equations.symbols: mu energy density; p_alpha principal stresses

key_equations.name: Weak energy condition
key_equations.meaning: Measured energy density is non-negative; implies null convergence.

key_equations.name: Weak energy condition for standard matter
key_equations.meaning: Equivalent statement of the weak energy condition for standard matter: non-negative density and non-negative sum of density with each principal stress.

key_equations.name: Generic condition
key_equations.meaning: Somewhere along every causal geodesic the tidal curvature seen by it is non-trivial.
key_equations.symbols: v^a tangent vector

key_equations.name: Hawking temperature
key_equations.meaning: Black-body temperature of a Schwarzschild hole, inversely proportional to mass (about 6x10^-8 K for one solar mass).
key_equations.symbols: The accompanying text writes (M/M_sun) x 6x10^-8 K; the dependence should be (M_sun/M).

figures.label: Fig. 20.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: The two real null legs l and n drawn relative to T and X.
figures.visual_description: Four arrows leave a common origin: T^a straight up, the spatial leg X^a horizontal to the right (its label is rendered as a small italic glyph that looks like i^a), l^a up and to the right at 45 degrees and n^a up and to the left at 45 degrees, so l and n bisect the angles between T and plus or minus X like light-cone generators.
figures.what_it_teaches: Null legs are the light-cone directions obtained by adding and subtracting a unit timelike and a unit spacelike vector.

redesign.idea: Tetrad builder: a 2D T-X diagram with a light cone plus a 3D inset of the transverse Y-Z plane where m = (Y + iZ)/sqrt2 is shown as a rotating phasor.
redesign.interaction: Drag a boost slider to see l and n rescale oppositely (l -> e^psi l, n -> e^-psi n) while l.n = 1 stays fixed; spin the Y-Z phase to show m -> e^{i chi} m; a live readout of the frame metric matrix confirms it never changes.

figures.label: Fig. 20.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: A primed coordinate frame turning about the shared z-axis of an unprimed one.
figures.visual_description: 3D perspective axes x, y, z with a dashed rotated pair x', y' sharing the vertical z = z' axis; a circular arrow at the top of the axis is marked phi-dot = a. A point P is connected to the axis by a horizontal segment of length r and lies at height z; arcs at the origin mark the azimuths phi and phi' measured from x and x'; small curved arrows at the ends of x' and y' indicate their rotation.
figures.what_it_teaches: The coordinate change phi' = phi - at to a uniformly rotating frame, used to show that rotation generates a dt dphi cross term.

redesign.idea: Rotating-frame metric lab: a turntable view of flat space beside the live line element in the rotating coordinates, next to the Kerr Boyer-Lindquist g_tphi at the same radius.
redesign.interaction: Slider for rotation rate; hover a point to show g_tt = 1 - a^2 r^2 and g_tphi; a marker shows the light cylinder where g_tt changes sign, compared with the Kerr ergosphere boundary as the learner raises the spin.

figures.label: Fig. 20.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Nested surfaces of Kerr: horizons, stationary limit surface, ring singularity.
figures.visual_description: A meridional cross-section drawn in perspective with axes y (horizontal) and z (vertical, labelled symmetry axis theta = 0) and a slanting third axis. The outermost oblate oval is the stationary limit (infinite-redshift) surface S^+; just inside it a rounder oval is the outer event horizon r = r^+, touching S^+ at top and bottom so that two dotted crescents on left and right mark the ergosphere. Much further in, a small oval is the inner horizon r = r^- with the infinite-redshift surface S^- inside it, and at the centre a zigzag ellipse in the equatorial plane represents the ring singularity.
figures.what_it_teaches: The geometry of Kerr's special surfaces: S_+ outside r_+ except at the poles, the ergosphere as the gap, the inner horizon and S_- deep inside, and the singularity as a ring.

redesign.idea: Spin-dial anatomy of a Kerr black hole: a 3D cutaway of S_+, r_+, r_-, S_- and the ring drawn in Kerr-Schild Cartesian coordinates, updating as a/m changes.
redesign.interaction: Slider a/m from 0 to 1 (and optionally beyond): watch the ergosphere grow from nothing to reach r = m at the poles and 2m at the equator, the horizons merge at a = m and vanish beyond, leaving a naked ring; toggle Boyer-Lindquist versus Cartesian embedding; click a surface to see its defining equation (g_00 = 0 or Delta = 0).

figures.label: Fig. 20.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two-dimensional spacetime diagram of sub-extremal Kerr in advanced Eddington-Finkelstein-type coordinates.
figures.visual_description: Vertical axis t-bar, horizontal axis r, with r = 0 marked on the left axis. Two vertical lines at r = r^- and r = r^+ divide the plane into regions III (left), II (middle), I (right). A family of parallel straight lines slopes down to the right at 45 degrees (ingoing principal null geodesics). A second family of curves (outgoing principal geodesics) bends: in region I they head up and out to the right, in region II they fall back toward r = r^-, and in region III they curve up and to the left. Small light cones (ellipses) are drawn where the families meet, tipping over as they approach and cross the horizons.
figures.what_it_teaches: Light-cone tilting across both horizons: outside r_+ outgoing light escapes, between horizons all light moves to smaller r, and inside r_- outgoing light can again increase r - a picture analogous to Reissner-Nordstrom.

redesign.idea: Light-cone field plot for Kerr in ingoing coordinates computed from (20.22) on the axis or equator.
redesign.interaction: Slider for a/m; click anywhere to launch the local outgoing and ingoing principal null rays and drop a light cone; animate a cone moving inward to see it tip at r_+ and right itself past r_-; compare panel with RN at matching r_+/-.

figures.label: Fig. 20.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Equatorial-plane spatial picture of sub-extremal Kerr showing how light fronts are displaced.
figures.visual_description: Concentric circles viewed from above: an outer dotted annulus is the ergosphere, bounded outside by the stationary limit surface S_+ and inside by the event horizon r = r^+; a further circle marks r = r^-, and a wavy circle at the centre is the ring singularity. Outside the ergosphere, small circles each have a dot at their centre (the emitter lies inside its own wavefront). On and inside S_+ the circles are shifted so that the dot sits on or beyond the edge in the direction of rotation. Between the horizons and inside, small triangles/wedges indicate wavefronts displaced inward. A curved arrow on the right shows the sense of rotation.
figures.what_it_teaches: Where an emitter can stay put (outside S_+), where it must co-rotate (ergosphere), and where it must also fall inward (inside r_+).

redesign.idea: Flash-bulb map of the equatorial plane: click to emit a short light pulse and watch the expanding wavefront computed from the local light cone, displaced by dragging.
redesign.interaction: Slider for a/m; click to fire; a colour overlay shows whether the emitter is inside its own wavefront; rotate to a counter-rotating rocket mode that shows the maximum achievable dphi/dt from (20.70).

figures.label: Fig. 20.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram of the maximally extended sub-extremal Kerr solution along the axis.
figures.visual_description: A vertical chain of diamonds with dashed r = const curves inside. Diamonds labelled I sit on the left and right, bounded by null edges marked scri-plus and scri-minus and annotated r = infinity. Between successive pairs of I regions lie diamonds labelled II. Above and below, regions labelled III contain thick timelike curves annotated r = 0 which lead across to further regions marked r = -infinity with their own scri boundaries. Labels r = r^+ and r = r^- mark the null boundaries between I and II and between II and III. The pattern repeats indefinitely up and down.
figures.what_it_teaches: The causal structure of eternal Kerr: infinitely many asymptotic regions, trapped regions II, timelike avoidable ring in regions III, and passage to negative r.

redesign.idea: Explorable Kerr conformal diagram with a world-line pen.
redesign.interaction: Draw a timelike path; the app refuses non-causal strokes, labels each region crossed, flags when the path passes r = 0 into negative r, and highlights region III where closed timelike curves exist; a toggle shows Schwarzschild and RN diagrams for comparison.

figures.label: Fig. 20.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram of extremal Kerr (a^2 = m^2) along the axis.
figures.visual_description: A zigzag column of diamonds: region I diamonds on the right each bounded by scri-plus and scri-minus (annotated r = infinity); region III diamonds on the left each containing a thick timelike line r = 0; the shared null boundaries are labelled r = m. There are no region II diamonds. The column continues indefinitely up and down with dashed r = const curves.
figures.what_it_teaches: When the horizons merge the trapped region disappears, leaving an alternation of exterior and interior regions like extreme Reissner-Nordstrom.
